question.explanation:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{16-x^2}}\,\textrm{d}x &= \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{16\cdot (1-x^2/16)}}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2/16}}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/4)^2}}\,\textrm{d}x \end{align*}

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine, \[ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin(u)+C. \]

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u = \dfrac x 4.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{1}{4} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x =4\,\textrm{d}u. \]

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{16-x^2}} \textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{1}{4} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-\left(x/4\right)^2}}\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & =\dfrac{1}{4} \int \dfrac {1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} \cdot (4\,\textrm{d}u) \\[5pt] & =\int \dfrac {\textrm{d}u}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} \\[5pt] & =\arcsin u + C \\[5pt] & = \arcsin \left(\dfrac x 4 \right) + C } \end{eqnarray}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent, \[ \int \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u = \arctan{u} + C. \]

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $9x^2=(3x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x =\dfrac{1}{3}\,\textrm{d}u. \]

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

$x$ $0$ $\dfrac13$
$u$ $0$ $1$

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align} \int_{0}^{1/3} \dfrac{2}{1+9x^2}\, \textrm{d}x &= 2 \int_{0}^{1/3} \dfrac{1}{1+(3x)^2}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} \, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac {2}{3} \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac {2}{3}\arctan{u} \, \Bigg|_{0}^{1}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac {2}{3}\left(\arctan(1) - \arctan(0) \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-0\right) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\pi}{6}} \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows: \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{3\sqrt3} \dfrac{15}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}\, \textrm{d}x &= 15\int_{0}^{3\sqrt3} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{36\cdot (1-x^2/36)}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{15}{6}\int_{0}^{3\sqrt3} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2/36}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{2}\int_{0}^{3\sqrt3} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/ 6)^2}}\, \textrm{d}x \end{align*}

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine, \[ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\textrm{d}u = \arcsin{u} + C. \]

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac{x}{6}\right)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u = \dfrac{x}{6}.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{6} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = 6\,\textrm{d}u. \]

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

$x$ $0$ $3\sqrt3$
$u$ $0$ $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align} \int_{0}^{3\sqrt3} \dfrac{15}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{5}{2} \int_{0}^{3\sqrt3} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/ 6)^2}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{2} \int_{0}^{{\sqrt3}/{2}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} \cdot 6 \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= 15 \int_{0}^{{\sqrt3}/{2}} \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} \\[5pt] &=15 \arcsin{u} \, \Bigg|_{0}^{{\sqrt3}/{2}} \\[5pt] &=15 \arcsin\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) - 15 \arcsin(0) \\[5pt] & = 15 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{3}\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{5\pi} \end{align}

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $9x^2 = (3x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x =\dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u. \]

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

$x$ $0$ $4$
$u$ $0$ $12$

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{0}^{4} \dfrac{12}{3+27x^2}\, \textrm{d}x &= 4 \int_{0}^{4} \dfrac{1}{1+(3x)^2}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 4 \int_{0}^{12} \dfrac{1}{1+u^2}\, \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{3} \int_{0}^{12} \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{1+u^2} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{4}{3} \arctan{ u}\Big|_{0}^{12}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{4}{3}\arctan{ \left(12\right)} - \dfrac {4}{3}\arctan{ (0)} \\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{4}{3}} \, \arctan\!{\left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{12}\right)} } \]

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent, \[ \int \frac{1}{1+u^2}\textrm{d}u =\arctan u +C. \]

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $4x^2=(2x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u = 2x.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x =\dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u. \]

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

$x$ $0$ $1$
$u$ $0$ $2$

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1 + 4x^2} \, \textrm{d}x & = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{1 + (2x)^2}\\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac {1}{1 + u^2} \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac {\textrm{d}u}{1 + u^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac 1 2 \arctan u \Big|_{0}^{2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac 1 2 \arctan(2) - \dfrac{1}{2}\arctan(0) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac 1 2 \arctan(2) } \end{eqnarray}

example.title: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Trigonometric Functions

question.explanation:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int_{0}^{8} \dfrac{1}{16 + x^2} \, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{0}^{8} \dfrac{1}{16\cdot (1+ x^2/16)} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac1{16}\int_{0}^{8} \dfrac{1}{1+ x^2/16} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac1{16}\int_{0}^{8} \dfrac{1}{1+ (x/4)^2} \, \textrm{d}x \end{align*}

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent, \[ \int \frac{1}{1+u^2}\textrm{d}u =\arctan u +C. \]

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u = \dfrac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{1}{4} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x =4\,\textrm{d}u. \]

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

$x$ $0$ $8$
$u$ $0$ $2$

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \int_{0}^{8} \dfrac{1}{16 + x^2} \, \textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{1}{16} \int_{0}^{8} \dfrac{1}{1+ (x/4)^2}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac 1 {16} \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac {1}{1 + u^2} \cdot (4\,\textrm{d}u) \\[5pt] & =\dfrac 1 4 \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac {\textrm{d}u}{1 + u^2} \\[5pt] & =\dfrac 1 4 \arctan u\Big|_{0}^{2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{4}(\arctan(2) - \arctan(0)) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{4}\arctan(2) } \end{eqnarray}
